deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematical derivation on this page. It continues Riemann's epistemological sketch for the natural-philosophy fragments (published in Weber's edition of the Gesammelte Werke among the philosophical fragments, the 'Erkenntnisstheoretisches' material). The argument runs as follows.

(a) Conclusion of the parenthesis from the previous page. Herbart is said to have shown that the concepts used to grasp the world, insofar as they are more than mere forms for connecting simple sense-presentations, can be derived from experience by the same process of concept formation. They therefore do not need to be traced, as Kant's categories are, to a constitution of the soul presupposed before all experience.

(b) Why this matters. Only by showing this origin in sense perception can the meaning of these concepts be fixed in a way adequate for natural science. Riemann restricts himself to what is necessary and does not set out the psychological process in full.

(c) Two modes of concept formation:
 1. formation of concepts from perceptions by abstraction;
 2. transformation or completion of concepts already formed, in order to remove contradictions or improbabilities.
 There is then a gap, marked '((Lücke))' by the transcriber.

(d) Application: continuity and causality. Once the concept of self-subsisting things exists, reflection on change produces a task, because change contradicts self-subsistence. The task is to keep this proven concept as far as possible. From this arise simultaneously:
 - the concept of continuous change, and
 - the concept of causality.
 What we observe is only a transition of a thing from one state (or 'mode of determination') to another without a perceptible jump. In completing the perceptions there are two hypotheses:
 (i) the transition consists of a very large but finite number of jumps, each imperceptible to our senses (a step function with tiny steps);
 (ii) the thing passes through all intermediate stages (a continuous path).
 The strongest reason for (ii) is the demand to preserve self-subsistence as far as possible. Riemann admits that a passage through all intermediate stages cannot actually be pictured, but notes this is strictly true of all concepts.

(e) Bridge to causality, continued on the next page. By the earlier, empirically proven concept of self-subsistence one infers that a thing would remain what it is if nothing else were added. Hence every change demands a cause, i.e. a principle of inertia or persistence motivates the search for causes.

Modern gloss (mine): hypotheses (i) and (ii) correspond to modelling a state trajectory as a fine step function versus a continuous function. Observation at finite resolution cannot decide between them. The choice of the continuum is justified methodologically (concept preservation), not empirically.
errors: No mathematical errors; the page is philosophical. Riemann himself flags the epistemic gap: the continuum hypothesis (ii) is not empirically distinguishable from (i), and passage through all intermediate stages cannot be represented. This is an acknowledged limitation, not an error.

results.what: Herbart-style derivation of world-concepts from experience via abstraction and via revising concepts to remove contradictions/improbabilities, opposed to Kantian a priori categories
results.modern_name: Empiricist/Herbartian concept formation; concept revision driven by anomaly (cf. later theory-change accounts)
results.usually_credited_to: J. F. Herbart (Metaphysik, Psychologie als Wissenschaft, 1820s); Riemann's version published by Weber/Dedekind 1876

results.what: Continuous change chosen over a finite sequence of imperceptible jumps, justified by preserving the concept of self-subsisting things; causality derived from the same concept
results.modern_name: Methodological justification of the continuum hypothesis for physical states; persistence/inertia principle as the origin of causal inquiry
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (published in Gesammelte Werke, philosophical fragments, 1876); related ideas in Herbart and Leibniz

deep.surprise_reason: This passage is part of Riemann's natural-philosophy fragments printed in the Gesammelte mathematische Werke (Weber/Dedekind, 1876). The content (Herbart vs Kant, continuity and causality from 'für sich bestehende Dinge') is known and discussed in the Riemann/Herbart literature. It contains no mathematics.

'des für sich Bestehens' at the top of the change paragraph: the image is consistent with 'des für sich Bestehens', as in the transcription; same form later ('des für sich Bestehens der Dinge').
